extractedText: MarketsWikiNewsSearchVideosEventsLog in/ Sign upenBTC Mining Companies' Transformation: Selling BTC to Fund AI – Where is the Battle for Hashrate Headed?JinseFinance2026/03/30 13:04FollowAuthor: Shaurya Malwa, Co-Head of Token & Data Asia Team at CoinDesk; Translation: xz@Jinse FinanceKey Information You Need to Know:Listed Bitcoin mining companies are facing an unsustainable economic model, losing approximately $19,000 for every Bitcoin produced, and are therefore rapidly shifting towards artificial intelligence and high-performance computing infrastructure.Mining companies have signed AI and high-performance computing contracts worth over $70 billion, and some mining companies expect 70% of their revenue to come from AI businesses by the end of 2026, essentially transforming into a business model primarily focused on operating data centers, with Bitcoin mining as a secondary activity.Mining companies have signed AI and high-performance computing contracts worth over $70 billion, and some mining companies expect 70% of their revenue to come from AI businesses by the end of 2026, essentially transforming into a business model primarily focused on operating data centers, with Bitcoin mining as a secondary activity. This transformation, fueled by massive borrowing and a large-scale sell-off of Bitcoin, has led to a decline in network hashrate and strained network security, making the future of the entire industry dependent on whether the price of Bitcoin can recover to around $100,000. The Bitcoin mining industry is undergoing its most fundamental transformation in history, and the clearest sign is not hashrate or difficulty adjustments, but rather the balance sheets of companies. CoinShares' Q1 2026 Mining Report, released this week, shows that in Q4 2025, the weighted average cash cost for publicly traded mining companies to produce one Bitcoin had risen to approximately $79,995. Bitcoin is trading between $68,000 and $70,000, and a CoinDesk report last week estimated that miners are losing approximately $19,000 for every BTC they mine. These figures are unsustainable, and the industry is well aware of this. The response is that the entire industry is shifting towards AI infrastructure—redefining the very nature of these companies. According to a CoinShares report, the total value of AI and high-performance computing (HPC) contracts announced by listed mining companies has exceeded $70 billion. CoreWeave's expanded partnership with Core Scientific alone is worth $10.2 billion over 12 years. TeraWulf has signed HPC contracts worth $12.8 billion. Hut 8 signed a 15-year, $7 billion AI infrastructure lease agreement for its River Bend campus. Cipher Digital has entered into a multi-billion dollar partnership with Fluidstack, a company invested in by Google. By the end of 2026, listed mining companies are projected to derive up to 70% of their revenue from AI, compared to approximately 30% currently. Core Scientific's AI hosting revenue already accounts for 39% of its total revenue, TeraWulf 27%, and IREN 9%, and is rapidly expanding—its under-construction liquid-cooled GPUs can reach up to 200 megawatts of computing power. This means that these mining companies are increasingly transforming into data center operators, with Bitcoin mining gradually becoming a secondary business. The economics explain this. According to CoinShares analysis, the cost per megawatt of Bitcoin mining infrastructure is approximately $700,000 to $1 million, while the cost per megawatt of AI infrastructure is between $8 million and $15 million—a significant difference, but AI businesses offer a more structurally sound and stable return. The **hashrate price**, a key indicator of a mining company's revenue per unit of computing power, fell to a post-halving low in early March, at approximately $28 to $30 per petahash per day. At this level, mining companies using previous-generation hardware needed to keep electricity costs below $0.05 per kilowatt-hour to maintain cash profits. Meanwhile, AI infrastructure contracts can promise profit margins of over 85% and provide visible revenue for several years. The report indicates that this transformation is primarily financed through two methods, both with clearly traceable data. First, debt financing. The overall leverage structure of the industry has fundamentally changed. IREN currently has $3.7 billion in five series of convertible notes. TeraWulf's total debt reached $5.7 billion, divided into convertible notes and senior secured notes at the computing business level. Cipher Digital issued $1.7 billion in senior secured notes in November, causing its quarterly interest expense to surge from $3.2 million in the first three quarters to $33.4 million in the fourth quarter. This type of debt far exceeds that of the traditional mining industry, representing infrastructure-level investments betting on the rapid monetization of AI revenue to repay the debt. Secondly, there was a Bitcoin sell-off.
